stories.title: The Night the Sea Went Dark

pages.text: Lama had always thought the Red Sea had no more secrets to show her. Her family had spent every winter holiday at her grandfather's house near Yanbu since she was a baby, and she knew every rock on the beach. But on the first night of this holiday, as she walked along the shore with her younger brother Faisal, something extraordinary happened. Each time a wave broke, it lit up with a cold, electric blue. Faisal grabbed her arm and whispered, "Lama, the sea is on fire!"

It wasn't fire, of course, and Lama, who dreamed of becoming a marine biologist, knew exactly what it was. "It's called bioluminescence," she explained, kicking the water so that bright sparks flew around her feet. "Tiny living things called plankton make their own light whenever something disturbs them." Faisal ran into the shallow water, laughing as his footprints glowed behind him. Their grandfather watched from the sand and smiled. "When I was a boy, fishermen used this light to find fish at night," he said. "We called it the sea's lanterns."

The glowing continued for several nights, but on the fourth night Lama noticed something strange. Near an old concrete pipe that stuck out of the sand, the water stayed completely dark, while on either side the waves sparkled as brightly as ever. "Maybe the plankton just don't like it there," Faisal suggested with a shrug. Lama wasn't convinced, and she couldn't get the dark patch out of her head. When she mentioned the pipe at dinner, her grandfather frowned. "That wasn't there when I was young," he said. "They built it a few years ago, when the new factory opened further up the coast."

Lama decided to investigate. She remembered her science teacher's favourite advice: a good scientist never jumps to conclusions. Over the next three days, she collected water samples in clean jars from five different points along the beach, labelling each one carefully. She measured the temperature with a thermometer borrowed from her grandfather's kitchen and tested the water with some pH strips left over from a school project. Faisal, who had been complaining that he was bored, soon became her most enthusiastic assistant.

The results were clearer than she had expected. The water near the pipe was almost three degrees warmer than anywhere else, and it was slightly more acidic. When she shook the jars in a dark room, the samples from further along the beach flashed with tiny blue lights, but the jar from the pipe remained dark. "Something coming out of that pipe is killing them," Lama said quietly. Faisal looked worried. "Then what about the fish? And the coral?"

Lama knew she couldn't solve this problem on her own. Her father suggested contacting the marine research centre at a university on the coast, but she hesitated. "Why would real scientists listen to a fourteen-year-old?" she asked. "Because your data is good," her father replied. "Evidence doesn't care how old you are." That night, she wrote a careful email and attached her notes, her photographs and a simple graph showing the temperature at each point.

For two days there was no reply, and Lama began to lose hope. Then, on the morning they were due to drive home to Riyadh, her phone buzzed. A researcher called Dr Noura Al-Harbi had written back to say that her team had been worried about this part of the coast for months but hadn't yet had the chance to study it. "Your observations could save us weeks of work," she wrote. "Would you be able to show us the exact location this afternoon?" Lama read the message three times before she could believe it.

The researchers arrived with equipment Lama had only ever seen in documentaries, including underwater sensors and special sampling bottles. They discovered that the factory was releasing hot water, used to cool its machines, straight into the sea, and that the water contained chemicals which should have been removed first. Dr Noura explained that warm, polluted water could badly damage coral reefs long before anyone noticed. "The plankton were your early warning system," she told Lama. "Most people would have walked past that dark water without thinking twice."

Months later, back in Riyadh, Lama received an email with wonderful news: the factory had been ordered to install a new system to cool and clean its water before it reached the sea. Dr Noura had also invited her to spend a week at the research centre the following summer. When the family returned to Yanbu that winter, Lama and Faisal hurried down to the beach on the very first night. As the waves rolled in beside the old pipe, they burst into brilliant blue light. "The lanterns are back," their grandfather said softly, and Lama smiled, knowing she had helped to bring them home.

questions.q: Why did part of the sea near the old pipe stay dark?
options: Hot, polluted water from the factory was killing the plankton
The water there was too deep for plankton to live
Faisal had frightened the plankton away

questions.q: What does the word "hesitated" mean in the sentence "she hesitated"?
options: She agreed immediately
She paused because she felt unsure
She became very angry

questions.q: How did Lama test whether the plankton were alive in each sample?
options: She looked at them under a microscope
She shook the jars in a dark room to see if they glowed
She sent them to her science teacher

questions.q: What did Lama's father mean when he said, "Evidence doesn't care how old you are"?
options: Young people should not try to do science
Good data is valuable no matter who collects it
Scientists only trust older researchers

questions.q: Why did Dr Noura call the plankton an "early warning system"?
options: Their disappearance showed a problem before the coral was badly damaged
They made a loud noise when the water was polluted
Fishermen used them to predict the weather

stories.title: The Parrot Who Knew Too Much

pages.text: When Uncle Khalid flew to Riyadh for a week-long conference, he left his African grey parrot, Sultan, with Omar's family in Jeddah. "Just one warning," he said at the door, looking unusually serious. "If Sultan hears something twice, he'll repeat it forever, and he copies voices perfectly." Omar, who was fourteen and thought he knew everything about animals, just laughed. By the end of the week, he would have given anything to take that laugh back.

That evening, Omar was practising a speech for Sunday's school assembly while Sultan watched him from his cage. Bored, Omar began imitating the head teacher, Mr. Hamdan, whose assemblies were famous for lasting forever. "And finally, students," he said in a deep, slow voice, "and finally... and finally..." Then he added in his own voice, "Honestly, wake me up when he finishes!" Meanwhile, his sister Reem was teaching the parrot to shout "Where is my phone?" in exactly the way their mother did every morning.

The next day at lunch, Dad made an announcement that almost made Omar choke on his rice. "My old university friend is coming to dinner on Thursday," he said proudly. "You know him, actually, Omar. It's Mr. Hamdan, your head teacher!" Omar's spoon froze halfway to his mouth. Across the room, Sultan tilted his head and quietly said, "And finally..."

For three days, Omar tried desperately to make the parrot forget what he had heard. He played nature documentaries, read poetry aloud and repeated "Mr. Hamdan is wonderful" until his throat hurt. Sultan simply ignored him and asked, "Where is my phone?" By Thursday afternoon, Omar had run out of ideas, so he carried the cage up to his bedroom and closed the door. "Stay quiet," he begged, as if the bird could understand a deal.

Mr. Hamdan arrived exactly on time, carrying a box of dates and smiling warmly. At dinner, he talked about the history of the school, then about his garden, then about the history of his garden. Just as he paused to drink his tea, a muffled voice floated down the stairs: "And finally... and finally!" Dad looked confused, but Omar quickly said it was the television. Under the table, his knees were shaking.

Unfortunately, nobody had told Omar's six-year-old brother, Hamza, about the plan. Delighted to have a guest, he ran upstairs and came back carrying the cage with both arms. "Look, Mr. Hamdan! He can talk!" he announced. Sultan looked straight at the head teacher and said, in Omar's voice, "Honestly, wake me up when he finishes!" The room fell so silent that Omar could hear the fridge humming in the kitchen.

Omar was getting ready to apologise for the rest of his life when Mr. Hamdan suddenly burst out laughing. He laughed so hard that he had to wipe his eyes with his napkin. "My wife has been telling me the same thing for twenty years," he admitted. At that moment, Sultan decided to join the fun and screamed, "Where is my phone?" in a voice that was unmistakably Mum's. Now it was Mum's turn to go red, while Reem pretended to study the ceiling.

After dessert, Mr. Hamdan took Omar aside, and Omar braced himself for the worst. "I'd like to make you an offer," the head teacher said with a twinkle in his eye. "If I keep Sunday's assembly under two minutes, you'll give your speech without notes and with real confidence." Omar was so relieved that he agreed before he had even thought about it. They shook hands, and Sultan, watching them, whistled as if he had arranged the whole thing.

On Sunday, Mr. Hamdan spoke for exactly ninety seconds, said "And finally" only once, and received the loudest applause in the school's history. Then Omar delivered his speech, and although his hands trembled at first, he finished to cheers. When Uncle Khalid came back that evening, Sultan greeted him with a brand-new phrase: "Excellent speech, Omar!" Uncle Khalid raised his eyebrows. "Did you teach him that?" he asked. Omar just smiled; he had finally learned to be careful about what he said twice.

questions.q: Why did Uncle Khalid warn the family about Sultan?
options: Because Sultan repeats anything he hears twice and copies voices
Because Sultan bites people he doesn't know
Because Sultan refuses to eat when he is away from home

questions.q: Where did Omar hide Sultan before the dinner?
options: On the roof
In his bedroom
In the kitchen

options: He relaxed completely
He prepared for something unpleasant
He ran away quickly

questions.q: Why did Mum go red at the dinner?
options: Sultan copied her voice asking for her phone
She burned the dessert
Mr. Hamdan criticised her cooking

questions.q: What can we infer from the ending of the story?
options: Omar decided never to give a speech again
Omar had secretly taught Sultan a kind phrase by repeating it
Uncle Khalid was angry that Sultan had learned new words

pages.text: Every summer, Yousef spent two weeks with his grandfather on the Farasan Islands, where the Red Sea was so clear that you could count the fish from the boat. His grandfather, Abu Saleh, had been a fisherman for over fifty years, and he could read the water the way other people read a newspaper. "The sea always tells you what it's going to do," he liked to say, "but only if you're patient enough to listen." Yousef, who was fourteen and usually glued to his phone, had never been particularly patient. This summer, however, something would happen that would change his mind.

On the third morning, Yousef and his cousin Omar took the small motorboat out to the reef to go snorkelling. Abu Saleh had warned them to come back before noon, because the wind usually picked up in the afternoon. The coral below them was breathtaking: purple fans swayed gently, and a school of silver fish flashed past like scattered coins. Then Omar grabbed Yousef's arm and pointed towards a dark shape near the edge of the reef. At first Yousef thought it was a rock, but then it moved.

It was a green sea turtle, larger than either of them, and it was trapped in an old fishing net. The net had obviously been abandoned long ago, because it was covered in seaweed and tiny shells. Every time the turtle struggled, the thin ropes cut deeper into its front flipper. "It can't reach the surface to breathe," Omar said, his voice shaking. Yousef knew that if they didn't act quickly, the turtle might drown.

They swam down together, but the net was tangled around a piece of coral, and their hands were useless against the tough nylon. Yousef remembered the small knife his grandfather kept in the boat for cutting fishing line. He raced back, his heart pounding, and returned with the knife held carefully in his hand. Working in short dives, they cut the ropes one by one, coming up for air whenever their lungs began to burn. By then, the sun was high, and the water was no longer as calm as it had been.

Finally, the last rope snapped, and the turtle rose slowly towards the surface, taking a long, noisy breath. However, its injured flipper hung at a strange angle, and it was clearly too weak to swim far. "We can't just leave it here," Yousef said. "If a shark doesn't find it, the waves will." Omar looked at the darkening sky and then at his cousin. "Then we'd better think fast," he replied.

Using a towel as a sling, they managed to lift the turtle into the boat, which was not easy since it weighed almost as much as both boys together. By the time they had started the engine, the waves had grown taller and white foam was breaking over the front of the boat. Yousef gripped the wheel and tried to remember everything his grandfather had taught him. "Don't fight the waves head-on," he heard the old man's voice say in his mind. "Meet them at an angle and let the sea carry you." Slowly and carefully, he steered them towards the shore.

Abu Saleh was waiting on the beach, and for a moment Yousef was sure they were in serious trouble. But when his grandfather saw the turtle, his stern expression softened. He called a friend who worked at the marine protection centre, and within an hour a team of volunteers had arrived to take the turtle away for treatment. "You came back late, and that was foolish," Abu Saleh said quietly. "But you saved a life today, and that is something I am proud of."

Over the following days, Yousef visited the centre whenever he could. The vet explained that the flipper would heal, although it would take several weeks. She also told him that thousands of abandoned nets, often called ghost nets, drift through the world's oceans, trapping turtles, dolphins and fish. "Rescuing one turtle might seem like a drop in the ocean," she said, "but every single one matters." Yousef asked if he could help, and soon he and Omar were spending their mornings clearing plastic and old rope from the beaches.

On the last day of his holiday, Yousef watched as the volunteers carried the turtle, now named Amal, which means hope, back to the water. A small tracking device had been attached to her shell so that scientists could follow her journey. She paused at the edge of the waves, as if she were saying goodbye, and then disappeared into the blue. Months later, back at school in Riyadh, Yousef received a message from the centre: Amal had been spotted laying her eggs on a beach in Farasan. He smiled, put his phone away, and thought about his grandfather's words, because he had finally learned to listen to the sea.

questions.q: Why did Abu Saleh tell the boys to return before noon?
options: Because the reef closed in the afternoon
Because the wind usually became stronger later in the day
Because he needed the boat for fishing

questions.q: In the sentence "his stern expression softened", what does "stern" mean?
options: Serious and strict
Tired and sleepy
Happy and excited

questions.q: What does the name "Amal" mean?
options: Ocean
Strength
Hope

questions.q: What does the vet mean when she says rescuing one turtle "might seem like a drop in the ocean"?
options: It is a very dangerous thing to do
It seems like a very small effort compared to the size of the problem
It is something that only happens in deep water

questions.q: Why does Yousef put his phone away at the end of the story?
options: Because his phone's battery has died
Because his teacher has told him to
Because the summer has changed him, and he now values the sea and his grandfather's advice

stories.title: The Most Patient Farmer in the Valley

pages.text: Every morning in the mountains near Abha, a thick white fog rolled over Grandfather Saleh's farm like a slow, silent river. Layla had watched it hundreds of times from her bedroom window, but this summer she saw it differently. The rain had been disappointing for two years in a row, and the old stone terraces, where her family had grown coffee and pomegranates for generations, were turning dusty and pale. "The fog is full of water," she thought, "so why does it simply disappear?"

That evening, she noticed something on the juniper tree beside the house: tiny drops hanging from its needles and falling one by one onto the ground. The soil under the tree was dark and damp, while everything around it was dry. "Grandfather, why is it always wet under this tree?" she asked. He smiled, stroking his grey beard. "The tree drinks from the clouds, my dear. My father used to say it was the most patient farmer in the valley."

Layla couldn't stop thinking about it. After hours of research online, she discovered that scientists in Chile and Morocco had built huge nets to catch fog, a technique known as fog harvesting. The school science fair was only six weeks away, and she had been searching for a project that actually mattered. She persuaded her older brother Faisal, who was always fixing bicycles in the garage, to help her. "If this doesn't work, you're washing my bike for a month," he joked, but she could tell he was curious.

Using wooden poles, plastic mesh from a hardware shop and a length of old pipe, they built their first fog collector on the edge of the highest terrace. The idea was simple: tiny droplets would hit the mesh, join together and slide down into a gutter that led to a bucket. The next morning, Layla ran outside before breakfast, her heart pounding. In the bucket there were nearly three litres of clear, cold water. She shouted so loudly that her mother came running, convinced something terrible had happened.

For a week, everything went perfectly, and Layla began recording the amount of water each day in a notebook. Then, one night, a violent wind swept down from the peaks. When she went out at dawn, she found the poles snapped in half and the mesh torn and tangled in a thorn bush. Layla sat down on the cold stones and felt tears sting her eyes. "We're back to square one," she whispered, "and the fair is in three weeks."

Grandfather found her there and sat beside her without saying a word for a long time. Finally, he pointed at the juniper tree, which had survived the same storm without losing a single branch. "Do you know why it didn't break?" he asked. "Its needles let the wind pass through, and its trunk bends instead of fighting." Layla stared at the tree, and slowly an idea began to form in her mind.

This time, she and Faisal designed a collector with flexible poles that could sway in strong winds, and a double layer of mesh with larger gaps so that air could escape. Layla also copied the shape of juniper needles, cutting thin vertical strips that guided the drops downward more quickly. They worked every afternoon after school, testing, failing and adjusting. Although the new design caught slightly less water on calm days, it survived two more storms without a scratch. "Grandfather would make a good engineer," Faisal admitted.

On the day of the fair, Layla stood nervously beside her model while a small machine blew mist across the mesh. The judges listened carefully as she explained how a tree, a storm and her grandfather's advice had shaped her invention. One judge, a professor from the university, asked how much water a full-sized version could produce. "Enough to water a whole terrace of coffee plants," Layla replied confidently, showing them her notebook full of measurements.

Layla won first prize, but the best moment came weeks later, when the university offered to help her build ten collectors across the family farm. By the end of winter, the terraces were green again, and Grandfather walked among the young coffee plants as proudly as a king. Neighbouring farmers began visiting to ask how they could build their own. When a local newspaper asked Layla who had invented her fog catcher, she laughed and pointed at the juniper tree. "Honestly," she said, "it was the most patient farmer in the valley. I just copied it."

questions.q: Why were the terraces on Grandfather Saleh's farm turning dusty and pale?
options: The family had stopped growing coffee.
There had been very little rain for two years.
The fog had become too thick for the plants.

questions.q: What gave Layla the first idea for her invention?
options: A video about fog nets in Chile
Her brother's bicycle repairs
Water dripping from the juniper tree

questions.q: When Layla says "We're back to square one", she means that...
options: they have to start again from the beginning.
they have finally finished the project.
they need to move the collector to another place.

questions.q: Why did the second fog collector survive the storms?
options: It was built from metal instead of wood.
Its poles could bend and air could pass through the mesh.
Faisal took it inside the house every night.

questions.q: Why does Layla point at the juniper tree at the end of the story?
options: She wants to show that her idea came from nature and her grandfather's wisdom.
She plans to cut down the tree to make more collectors.
She doesn't understand the journalist's question.

stories.title: The Suitcase with the Red Ribbon

pages.text: Yousef had been looking forward to the family trip to Malaysia for months. After an eight-hour flight from Riyadh, they finally landed in Kuala Lumpur just as the sun was rising over the hills. At the baggage carousel, Yousef spotted a dark blue suitcase with a red ribbon tied to the handle. His mother had tied that ribbon herself so they would never mix it up with anyone else's. He grabbed it confidently, and his father hurried everyone towards the taxis before the morning traffic built up.

At the hotel, Yousef unzipped the suitcase, eager to change out of his travel clothes. Instead of his shirts and trainers, he found brushes wrapped in soft cloth, rolls of thin paper and a heavy black ink stick. His heart sank. "Unless you've taken up painting overnight, that isn't yours," said his sister Huda, trying not to laugh. Yousef stared at the red ribbon on the handle, hardly able to believe that a stranger had chosen exactly the same idea.

Tucked inside the lid was an envelope with an invitation to a calligraphy exhibition at the Islamic Arts Museum. It was opening at four o'clock that afternoon, and the name printed under the word "Artist" was Aminah Rahman. Beneath the envelope lay a large sheet of paper covered in beautiful Arabic letters, but the final word had been left unfinished. Yousef realised that, without these tools, the artist might not be able to complete her work in time. When his father phoned the airport, the lost luggage office warned that returning bags could take several days.

"We were planning to visit the Petronas Towers today," his father said, glancing at his watch. "Finding one person in a city of millions is like looking for a needle in a haystack." Yousef pointed out that they already knew exactly where she would be at four o'clock. "If this were our suitcase, we would hope someone would make the effort," his mother added quietly. His father thought for a moment, then smiled and picked up his car keys. By then it was already half past two, and heavy tropical rain had begun to pour down outside.

Within ten minutes, their taxi was stuck in traffic that hardly moved at all. The driver, a cheerful man called Mr Lim, suggested they get out and walk the last part through a park, since it would be much quicker on foot. They hurried along the wet paths under two small umbrellas, while Yousef held the suitcase tightly against his chest to keep it dry. By the time the white domes of the museum appeared, his shoes were soaked through. On the bright side, the clock on his phone showed that they still had twenty minutes to spare.

Yousef was explaining the situation to the security guard when a small, elderly woman in a grey headscarf rushed across the entrance hall. To his astonishment, she was pulling a dark blue suitcase with a red ribbon on the handle. "I believe this belongs to you, young man!" she said, laughing. She had taken his bag by mistake at the airport and had found his name on a luggage label inside, so she had intended to return it after the opening. "It seems we both had the same clever idea about ribbons," she said with a wink.

Mrs Aminah explained that she always left the last word of her main piece unfinished on purpose. It was her tradition to complete it in front of her guests, so that they could share the moment with her. "Without my brushes, I was going to disappoint everyone," she admitted. Then she surprised Yousef by asking him to help her prepare the ink. He carefully rubbed the black ink stick against the stone with a little water until the liquid turned dark and smooth.

At exactly four o'clock, a crowd gathered around the table as Mrs Aminah dipped her brush into the ink. With a few graceful strokes, she completed the final word, and Yousef recognised it at once: سفر, meaning "journey." "A journey is never really finished until you share it with someone," she told the guests, looking directly at Yousef and his family. Everyone burst into applause, and Huda, who had been filming the whole time, whispered that it was the best thing she had ever recorded.

Before they left, Mrs Aminah handed Yousef a small card on which she had written his name in elegant Arabic script. That evening, the family finally stood beneath the shining Petronas Towers, which glowed like silver against the night sky. "Are you still disappointed that we lost half a day?" his father asked. Yousef shook his head, holding the card carefully in his pocket, and said it had been the best day of the whole trip. The next morning, he tied a second ribbon, a green one, to his suitcase handle, just in case.

questions.q: Why did Yousef take the wrong suitcase at the airport?
options: It looked exactly like his, including a red ribbon on the handle
His sister told him it was theirs
His father picked it up for him

questions.q: What did Yousef find inside the stranger's suitcase?
options: Clothes and a football shirt
Calligraphy tools and an invitation to an exhibition
A camera and a map of Kuala Lumpur

questions.q: In the story, "like looking for a needle in a haystack" means something is…
options: very dangerous
very easy to do
very difficult to find

questions.q: Why had Mrs Aminah left the last word of her piece unfinished?
options: She had run out of ink
It was her tradition to finish it in front of her guests
She did not know which word to write

questions.q: Why did Yousef tie a green ribbon to his suitcase at the end?
options: To avoid mixing up his bag with someone else's again
Because Mrs Aminah gave it to him as a gift
Because the red ribbon had been lost in the rain

pages.text: Yousef had been the top scorer at his school in Jeddah for two seasons, and everyone expected him to lead the team in the regional under-15 cup. Three weeks before the final, however, he landed badly during training and felt a sharp pain shoot through his ankle. The doctor's verdict was clear: no football for at least six weeks. Yousef nodded politely, but inside he felt as if the ground had disappeared beneath his feet. That evening, he pushed his boots to the back of his wardrobe and refused to look at them.

For days he avoided the training ground, and he ignored most of Omar's messages. "The team misses you," Omar said when Yousef finally answered the phone. "Even if you can't play, you could come and watch." "Watch?" Yousef replied bitterly. "Sitting on the side while everyone else plays isn't exactly my idea of fun." Later, his father, who had overheard the conversation, said quietly, "A player who only learns with his feet learns half the game."

The next afternoon, Coach Khalid handed Yousef a small blue notebook. "Your eyes still work perfectly," the coach said with a smile. "I want you to study our opponents: every habit, every weakness. Write it all down." Yousef wasn't convinced, but he took the notebook and limped up to the stands. Their opponents in the final, Al-Noor Academy, had a goalkeeper called Hamad who hadn't conceded a single penalty all season.

Over the next two weeks, Yousef watched recordings of Al-Noor's matches on his laptop until late at night. At first he noticed nothing unusual, and he began to wonder whether he was wasting his time. Then, during an old cup match, something caught his eye. Just before each penalty, Hamad tapped his left glove twice, and every time he did, he dived to the right. Yousef rewound the clip a dozen times to make sure he wasn't imagining it.

When Yousef showed him the notes, Coach Khalid raised his eyebrows. "Are you certain about this?" he asked. "I've checked eleven penalties," Yousef said. "He did it every single time." The coach studied the pages for a long moment before closing the notebook carefully. "Then this stays between us and the penalty takers, because if word gets out, it's worthless."

On the day of the final, the stadium was packed with families, and the afternoon heat hung over the pitch like a heavy blanket. Yousef sat on the bench in his team tracksuit, his crutches lying beside him. The match was tense from the very first whistle, and Al-Noor took the lead just before half-time. Twenty minutes from the end, Omar equalised with a powerful header. After extra time the score was still 1-1, which meant the cup would be decided by penalties.

As the players gathered in a circle, Yousef whispered the same advice to each penalty taker. "Keep your eyes on his left glove. If he taps it twice, shoot to the left." Omar, who had been chosen to take the fifth kick, was trembling. "What if I miss in front of everyone?" he asked. "Then at least you'll have tried," Yousef replied, "but trust me, you won't."

Both teams scored their first three penalties, but Al-Noor's fourth kick hit the crossbar and bounced away. If Omar scored, the cup would be theirs. As he placed the ball on the spot, the whole stadium seemed to hold its breath. Hamad bounced on his toes, then tapped his left glove twice. Omar kept his cool, sent the ball calmly into the left corner, and watched Hamad fly the wrong way.

Within seconds, Yousef's teammates had lifted him off the bench, crutches and all, while the crowd cheered and applauded. After the medals were presented, Hamad walked over and shook his hand. "Great game," he said with a puzzled smile. "But how did you know where to shoot?" Yousef laughed and held up his notebook. "I had six weeks to watch," he said, realising that his injury had been a blessing in disguise, and that from now on he would play with his eyes as well as his feet.

questions.q: Why couldn't Yousef play in the final?
options: He had injured his ankle during training.
The coach had dropped him from the team.
He had argued with Omar.

questions.q: What did Yousef discover about Hamad?
options: He always stayed in the middle of the goal.
He tapped his left glove twice before diving to the right.
He was afraid of powerful shots.

questions.q: In the story, the word "conceded" (page 3) is closest in meaning to:
options: saved
allowed to be scored
celebrated

questions.q: Why did Coach Khalid want to keep the secret between a few people?
options: He wanted to take the credit himself.
He didn't believe Yousef's notes were correct.
If Al-Noor found out, the information would no longer be useful.

questions.q: What can we infer about how Yousef's attitude changed by the end of the story?
options: He decided to give up football and become a coach.
He saw that his injury had taught him a valuable new way to understand the game.
He felt jealous that Omar scored the winning penalty.

stories.title: The Robot That Listened to Palm Trees

pages.text: Every summer, Huda spent the holidays at her grandfather's farm in Al-Ahsa, where thousands of date palms stood in long, quiet rows. This year, however, she had brought something unusual in her suitcase: a small six-legged robot that she had built herself, with a microphone as sensitive as a doctor's stethoscope. She had named it Sami. "What is that thing supposed to do?" her grandfather asked, raising an eyebrow over his glasses. "It listens," Huda replied proudly. "It can hear what's happening inside a tree."

Her grandfather laughed, but not unkindly. He had been growing dates for over fifty years, and he believed that no machine could understand palms better than a farmer's hands and eyes. Huda explained that the red palm weevil, a tiny insect, lays its eggs deep inside the trunk, where nobody can see them. By the time a farmer notices the damage, it is usually too late to save the tree. "But the young insects make a chewing sound while they eat," she said. "Sami has been trained to recognise it."

The next morning, before the heat became unbearable, Huda carried Sami out into the rows of palms. The robot climbed slowly up each trunk, pressed its microphone against the bark, and listened for a few seconds before moving on. For two hours, its small screen showed nothing but a green tick. Huda was beginning to wonder whether her whole project had been a waste of time. Then, at the forty-third tree, the screen suddenly flashed red.

"Grandfather!" she shouted, running back to the house. He followed her reluctantly, still holding his cup of Arabic coffee, and examined the tree carefully. "It looks perfectly healthy," he said, tapping the trunk. "Your robot must have made a mistake." Huda's heart sank, but she refused to give up. "Please," she begged, "could your workers just check it? If I'm wrong, I'll never mention Sami again."

That afternoon, two workers drilled a small hole into the trunk. Everyone held their breath as they pulled out the wood. Inside were dozens of pale, wriggling larvae, which had already eaten a tunnel nearly as long as Huda's arm. Her grandfather stared at them in silence for a long time. "If we had waited another month," he said quietly, "this tree would have fallen, and the insects would have spread to all the others."

From that day on, her grandfather treated Sami like a member of the team. Every morning, he walked beside Huda as the robot checked the trees, and he even gave it a nickname: "the little doctor." Over the next three weeks, Sami discovered weevils in eleven more palms, all of which were treated in time. Huda kept a detailed record of every result, because she had a plan. The national young inventors' competition in Riyadh was only a month away.

On the day of the competition, the hall was packed with students, teachers and judges. Huda's hands were shaking as she placed Sami on a real palm trunk that the organisers had provided. But when she pressed the button, nothing happened. The screen stayed black, because a wire had come loose during the long journey. With only ten minutes before the judges reached her table, she had no tools and no idea what to do.

Just then, a familiar voice came from behind her. "Did you really think I would miss this?" Her grandfather had driven all the way from Al-Ahsa, and he was holding a small toolbox and a thick folder. While Huda repaired the wire with trembling fingers, he spoke to the judges himself, showing them photographs of the infected trees and the record she had kept. "I have been a farmer for fifty years," he told them, "and this girl's robot taught me something new."

Sami came back to life just in time to climb the trunk and give a perfect demonstration. When the results were announced that evening, Huda's name was called for first place, and she could hardly believe her ears. On the drive home, her grandfather was already making plans to build ten more robots for the farmers in his village. Huda smiled and looked out at the golden desert. Somewhere out there, she thought, thousands of palm trees were waiting to be heard.

stories.title: The Night the Lights Went Out

pages.text: Every summer, Reem and her younger brother Omar spent two weeks with their grandfather in a quiet fishing village on the Farasan Islands. Grandfather had fished the Red Sea for more than fifty years, and he could read the water the way other people read a newspaper. This year, however, he had something more exciting than fish to show them. On the beach below his house, he had marked a small circle of stones. "Under this sand," he whispered, as if the beach might overhear, "more than a hundred hawksbill turtles are waiting to be born."

Grandfather explained that the mother turtle had laid her eggs almost two months earlier, and they would hatch any night now. "When the babies come out, they don't know where the sea is," he said. "They simply crawl towards the brightest horizon, which is normally the moonlight shining on the water." Omar rolled his eyes and joked that the turtles should just use a map app. Reem laughed, but she found herself looking at the dark, empty sea and wondering how something so small could be so brave.

Two nights later, a new café opened on the other side of the coastal road. It was a cheerful place, with colourful lanterns, strong cardamom coffee and a huge sign that glowed bright white across the sand. Families sat outside chatting, and children played until late. Grandfather was pleased for the owner, Abu Khalid, who had worked hard for years to open it. Reem, though, kept glancing from the dazzling sign to the circle of stones, and a worrying thought began to grow in her mind.

On the fourth night, Omar shouted from the beach, "The sand is moving!" The three of them hurried down and watched, hardly daring to breathe, as tiny flippers pushed up through the surface. Within minutes, dozens of baby turtles, each no bigger than a biscuit, were tumbling out of the nest. But instead of heading for the waves, they turned around as one. Slowly but determinedly, they began crawling up the beach, straight towards the road and the shining café.

"They think the café is the sea!" Reem cried. Omar wanted to pick them all up and carry them to the water, but Grandfather stopped him. "If they don't make the journey themselves, they may never remember this beach," he said firmly. "We need to give them back their moon." He ran to his boat and returned with an old sail, which he and Reem held up high like a wall between the turtles and the glaring lights.

Meanwhile, Grandfather sent Omar racing across the road to find Abu Khalid. Breathless, Omar explained everything, while curious customers turned to stare at the boy who had burst in without a word of greeting. Abu Khalid frowned and looked at his crowded tables. Switching off the lights on the busiest night of the week was hardly good for business. "Please," Omar begged. "If you don't, they'll end up on the road, and the cars won't even see them."

For a long moment, nothing happened. Then, all at once, the sign flickered and went dark, followed by every lantern in the café. Without the competition, the moon's silver path on the water seemed to grow brighter. On the sand, the little turtles hesitated, turned, and began scrambling towards the sea. It was a race against time, because ghost crabs were already appearing from their holes, hungry for an easy meal.

Reem lowered the sail and walked beside the hatchlings, gently waving away the crabs. One tiny turtle got stuck in a deep tyre track, struggling again and again to climb out. Reem longed to lift it, but she remembered Grandfather's words and waited, her heart in her mouth. At last, it pulled itself free and disappeared into a wave. Only then did she notice that the café customers had crossed the road and were standing quietly in the dark, and suddenly they all began to clap.

A week later, Abu Khalid replaced his white sign with soft orange lights pointing downwards, and he put up a notice asking visitors to keep the beach dark during hatching season. "My café can wait one night," he told Grandfather with a smile, "but those turtles could not." Grandfather explained that, if they survived, some of the females would return to this very beach in about twenty-five years to lay their own eggs. Reem did the maths and grinned. By then she would be almost forty, and she had already decided she would be standing right here, waiting to welcome them home.

examples: I see your point, although not all influencers are honest.
It depends on whether the influencer is being paid to advertise.
Although social media can be fun, it can also make people feel insecure.

words.ex: E-sports have become extremely popular in Saudi Arabia in recent years.
Some parents don't see gaming as a serious career path.
The gaming tournament in Riyadh attracted players from all over the world.
If you want to become a professional player, you have to take training seriously.
Top players earn money from sponsorship deals with big companies.
The gaming industry is highly competitive, so only a few players become famous.

dialogue.t: Should video games be taken seriously as a career?
Some people claim that gaming is just a waste of time, whereas others see it as a real profession.
What's your opinion?
There's no doubt that e-sports are growing fast in the region. Huge tournaments like the Esports World Cup in Riyadh offer millions of dollars in prizes.
So would you encourage a teenager to become a professional gamer?
On the one hand, it's an exciting career with sponsorship opportunities. On the other hand, it's highly competitive, and very few players succeed.
Some experts say gaming careers will soon be as normal as football careers.
I'm not entirely convinced that it will happen soon. I think young people should still finish their education as a backup plan.

grammar.title: Presenting both sides: whereas / on the one hand
grammar.ar: عند مناقشة موضوع من جانبين نستخدم whereas بمعنى «بينما» لربط رأيين مختلفين في جملة واحدة. ونستخدم On the one hand ... On the other hand بمعنى «من ناحية... ومن ناحية أخرى» لعرض الإيجابيات ثم السلبيات في جملتين منفصلتين. انتبه: لا تقل On the other side، فالعبارة الصحيحة هي On the other hand.
examples: Some people claim that gaming is harmful, whereas others say it improves problem-solving skills.
On the one hand, professional gamers can earn a lot. On the other hand, their careers are often very short.
My brother loves strategy games, whereas I prefer sports games.

words.ex: Many students use an AI tool to check their grammar.
If you rely on AI for every answer, you won't learn anything.
Copying an AI answer and calling it your own work is a form of plagiarism.
Teachers want students to develop critical thinking, not just copy information.
Our school has published clear guidelines on using technology in class.
It isn't fair if some students use AI to write their essays and others don't.

dialogue.t: Lots of students use AI tools for homework now. Is that a good thing?
It can be helpful, for example to explain a difficult maths problem. The problem with AI is that some students just copy the answers.
And what would happen in the long term?
If students relied too much on AI, they would lose their critical thinking skills.
So should schools ban AI completely?
No, I don't think so. Schools should be allowed to use AI as long as they have clear guidelines.
What kind of rules would you suggest?
It would be better if students had to explain how they used AI. That way it's fair, and it isn't plagiarism.

grammar.title: Second conditional and It would be better if
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثانية للحديث عن مواقف افتراضية أو متخيَّلة ونتائجها. التركيب هو: If + الماضي البسيط، ثم would + الفعل في صيغته الأساسية. ونستخدم It would be better if + الماضي البسيط لاقتراح فكرة أو تغيير، مع أننا نتحدث عن الحاضر أو المستقبل. لا تضع would بعد if مباشرة.
examples: If students relied too much on AI, they would forget how to write essays.
It would be better if teachers showed us how to use AI responsibly.
If our school banned AI, some students would still use it at home.

words.ex: After reading the article, I decided to reconsider my opinion.
There is strong evidence that sleep is affected by using phones at night.
That's a fair point – I didn't think about the cost.
My sister persuaded me to try reading books instead of watching videos.
Talking to older people can give you a different perspective.
A good debater is open-minded and listens to other opinions.

dialogue.t: Last time, you said online games were a complete waste of time. Do you still think so?
Well, I used to think that, but now I realise some games can actually be useful.
Here's a fact: research shows that some strategy games can improve problem-solving and teamwork skills.
That's a fair point – I hadn't considered teamwork. My cousin plays team games online and he communicates really well.
So would you say gaming is completely positive?
Having said that, I still believe that playing for more than two or three hours a day is unhealthy.
And there's evidence that gamers who take breaks perform better.
You've persuaded me that gaming can be beneficial, as long as players take regular breaks and stay balanced.

grammar.title: Talking about past opinions: used to and the past perfect
grammar.ar: نستخدم used to + الفعل في صيغته الأساسية للحديث عن رأي أو عادة كانت في الماضي ولم تعد موجودة الآن، مثل: I used to think. ونستخدم الماضي التام had/hadn't + التصريف الثالث للفعل للحديث عن شيء حدث (أو لم يحدث) قبل لحظة معيّنة في الماضي، مثل: I hadn't considered. انتبه: لا تقل I was used to think، فهذا خطأ شائع.
examples: I used to think AI was dangerous, but now I realise it can be helpful.
I hadn't considered how much time I spend on my phone until I checked the app.
She used to believe that influencers were always honest.

words.ex: My opponent made some strong arguments in the debate.
Some countries have decided to ban phones in schools.
In my rebuttal, I explained why my opponent's argument was weak.
Phones can reduce students' concentration in class.
Parents want their children to carry phones in case of emergency.
To sum up, I believe phones should be allowed only during breaks.

dialogue.t: Let's begin the debate. Please present your opening argument: should phones be banned in schools?
Yes, they should. My first argument is that phones are a huge distraction and reduce students' concentration in class.
Do you have a second point?
Furthermore, phones can lead to cyberbullying during the school day, which affects students' wellbeing.
But I'd say students need phones in case of emergency, so they can contact their parents.
My opponent suggested that phones are necessary for emergencies; however, students can always use the school office phone.
Thank you. Now, please give your conclusion.
To sum up, the evidence shows that schools without phones have better results and fewer behaviour problems, so a ban is the right decision.

grammar.title: Reporting someone's argument: suggest, claim, argue
grammar.ar: في المناظرات نحتاج إلى نقل ما قاله الطرف الآخر قبل الرد عليه. نستخدم أفعالاً مثل suggested that وclaimed that وargued that، ثم نكتب جملة كاملة. وعادةً نرجع زمن الفعل خطوة إلى الماضي، فـ is تصبح was وcan تصبح could. ثم نستخدم however للرد، ونضع قبلها فاصلة منقوطة أو نقطة، وبعدها فاصلة.
examples: My opponent suggested that phones were useful for research; however, computers in the library can do the same job.
She claimed that students could control themselves, but the evidence shows the opposite.
He argued that a ban would be unfair to responsible students.

words.ex: We've only got a budget of 500 riyals, so we need to spend it carefully.
According to the schedule, the flag ceremony starts at nine o'clock.
I think we should prioritise the decorations because they set the mood.
The school hall would be the perfect venue for the celebration.
Parents could help by bringing refreshments like dates and juice.
We'll need at least ten volunteers to set up the stage.

dialogue.t: So, we need to plan the National Day celebration. How about we start with the activities?
Good idea. Wouldn't it be a good idea to have a traditional food stall? Everyone loves that.
Definitely. But our budget is quite tight. I think we should prioritise the decorations because they make the biggest impression.
That makes sense. Maybe the food could be donated by parents, so it doesn't cost us anything.
Brilliant. What about the schedule? How about we begin with the national anthem at nine?
Sounds good. Then poetry and songs until eleven, and the food stall after that.
Perfect. Let's go with the school hall as the venue, shall we?
Yes, let's do that. It's big enough and it has a stage.

grammar.title: Making suggestions
grammar.ar: نستخدم عبارات مختلفة لتقديم الاقتراحات بأدب. بعد How about نستخدم الفعل مع ing أو نقول How about we + الفعل في صيغته الأساسية. أما Wouldn't it be a good idea يأتي بعدها to + الفعل، وهي طريقة مهذبة جداً. ونضيف shall we في نهاية الجملة بعد Let's لنطلب موافقة الطرف الآخر.
examples: How about having a poetry competition?
Wouldn't it be a good idea to invite the parents?
Let's go with the earlier start time, shall we?

words.ex: The main benefit of planting trees is that they give us shade in summer.
The only drawback of solar lights is that they're expensive to install.
Recycling bins on every street would be really effective.
A community garden needs regular maintenance, especially watering.
Using local plants is more sustainable because they need less water.
Cycling lanes might cost a lot now, but they'll save money in the long run.

dialogue.t: Let's look at these five ideas for making our neighbourhood greener. What about planting more trees?
The benefit of planting trees is that they provide shade and clean the air.
True, but the drawback would be the amount of water they need in our hot climate.
Fair point. What about a community garden?
I'm not sure a community garden would work because people might not have time to look after it.
Maybe. I think recycling bins would be more effective than a garden, actually.
I agree. They're cheap, and they need very little maintenance.
So recycling bins and trees are our top two, then?

grammar.title: Comparing options with would
grammar.ar: عندما نقيّم أفكاراً لم تحدث بعد، نستخدم would لأننا نتحدث عن نتائج افتراضية. ونستخدم more + الصفة الطويلة + than للمقارنة بين خيارين، مثل more effective than. ويمكن استخدام less للعكس، أو much لتقوية المقارنة.
examples: Solar panels would be more expensive than recycling bins.
A cycling lane would be much safer than riding on the road.
Planting trees would be less effective in the short term.

words.ex: After a long discussion, we finally reached a compromise.
My main priority is that the trip is educational.

words.ar: يلتقي في منتصف الطريق / يتنازل كل طرف قليلاً
words.ex: If you pay for the tickets, I'll pay for lunch, so we meet halfway.
That sounds like a reasonable price for a full-day trip.
The teacher insisted on visiting the museum first.
If the theme park is too expensive, is there a cheaper alternative?

dialogue.t: I really think the class trip should be to the science museum. It's educational.
I take your point, but most students would prefer something fun, like the water park.
I see where you're coming from, however the school wants the trip to be linked to our lessons.
OK. What if we went to the aquarium instead? It's fun, and we can learn about marine life.
That's interesting, but the aquarium is quite far away.
Maybe we could meet halfway by visiting the museum in the morning and the beach in the afternoon.
That's a reasonable compromise. I think both the students and the school would be happy.
Great, let's suggest that to the class.

grammar.title: Contrasting ideas: but and however
grammar.ar: نستخدم but و however لإظهار التناقض أو الرأي المخالف بأدب. تأتي but عادة في وسط الجملة لتربط بين جزأين. أما however فهي أكثر رسمية، وغالباً تأتي في بداية جملة جديدة وبعدها فاصلة، أو بعد فاصلة في وسط الجملة كما في الحديث. ومن الأخطاء الشائعة استخدام but و however معاً في الجملة نفسها.
examples: I take your point, but the museum is closed on Fridays.
The water park is fun. However, it's very expensive.
I see where you're coming from, however we need to think about the cost.

words.ex: Some students find it hard to cope with exam pressure.
My workload is huge this week because I have three tests.
If you procrastinate, you'll end up studying all night.
I felt overwhelmed when I saw how much revision I had to do.
It's easier to start a big project if you break it down into small steps.
The deadline for the group project is next Thursday.

dialogue.t: Lots of teenagers feel overwhelmed during exams. What would you suggest?
One way to deal with exam stress would be to make a realistic revision timetable.
Good idea. And it might help to take short breaks every hour.
Exactly. What about group projects where one person doesn't do any work?
If I were in that situation, I'd talk to that person privately first.
Yes, that's better than complaining to the teacher straight away.
The key thing is to sort out problems before the deadline gets too close.
Absolutely. Leaving it until the last minute only makes things worse.

grammar.title: Second conditional for advice
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثانية للحديث عن مواقف افتراضية أو لتقديم النصيحة. التركيب هو: If + الماضي البسيط، ثم would + الفعل الأساسي. في النصيحة نقول If I were وليس If I was، وهذا أكثر صحة في الامتحانات. لاحظ أنه لا نضع would في جزء if.
examples: If I were you, I'd start revising earlier.
If my friend felt stressed, I'd suggest going for a walk.
If we divided the tasks fairly, the project would be easier.

words.ex: Could you clarify what you mean by 'cheap'?
I understand your point of view, but I see it differently.
I'd like to build on your idea about online lessons.
That's interesting. Could you elaborate a little?
Sorry to interrupt, but I think we're running out of time.
In a good discussion, both speakers take turns and listen carefully.

dialogue.t: I think smartphones can actually help students learn. What do you think about using them in class?
Sorry, do you mean that students should use their own phones during lessons?
Yes, but only for specific tasks, like quick research or quizzes.
I see. Building on what you said, teachers could use apps to check understanding.
Exactly. Would you agree that there's also a risk of distraction, though?
Definitely. Some students would just check social media.
So maybe clear rules are the answer. What's your point of view on that?
I think rules are essential. Without them, it wouldn't work.

grammar.title: Questions that involve your partner
grammar.ar: للحفاظ على استمرار المحادثة نستخدم أسئلة تدعو الطرف الآخر للمشاركة. نستخدم What do you think about + اسم أو فعل مع ing لطلب الرأي. وWould you agree that + جملة كاملة لاقتراح فكرة بلطف. وللاستيضاح نقول Sorry, do you mean that + جملة كاملة، مع الحفاظ على ترتيب الجملة الخبرية بعد that.
examples: What do you think about having longer breaks?
Would you agree that homework helps us remember things?
Sorry, do you mean that we should cancel the trip?

words.ex: In the exam, you should always justify your opinions with reasons.
We need to reach a decision in the last minute of the task.
Good communication is essential for working in a team.
Let's narrow down the options to the two best ones.
On the whole, I think teenagers today are more independent.
The advantages of learning a language outweigh the difficulties.

dialogue.t: We need to decide which skill is the most useful for a teenager starting secondary school.
I think time management is the most important because you have so much more homework.
That's true, and making friends matters too. We both seem to agree that these two are essential.
Yes. But for me, time management outweighs friendship, because it affects your grades.
OK, I can accept that. So, have we decided that time management is the most useful?
Yes, let's go with that.
Now, a broader question. Do you think schools should teach life skills?
Generally speaking, I believe they should, because not every family has time to teach them at home.

grammar.title: Present perfect for checking decisions
grammar.ar: نستخدم المضارع التام (have/has + التصريف الثالث للفعل) للتأكد من قرار تم اتخاذه للتو، لأن نتيجته مهمة الآن. في السؤال نقدّم have على الفاعل: Have we decided...? ولتلخيص اتفاق الطرفين نستخدم We both seem to agree that + جملة. هذه العبارات مفيدة جداً في نهاية الجزء الثالث من امتحان B2 First.
examples: So, have we decided that the library is the best option?
We've chosen sport, but we haven't agreed on the second option yet.
We both seem to agree that money isn't the most important factor.

words.ex: Saudi Arabia is investing heavily in renewable energy, such as solar and wind power.
The tourism sector is growing fast thanks to projects like AlUla and the Red Sea.
Engineers need strong problem-solving skills to fix complex technical issues.
You'll need a university qualification in computer science to work as a software developer.
My cousin became an entrepreneur after starting her own app design company.
Doing an internship is a great way to get some work experience before you graduate.

dialogue.t: So, have you thought about what you want to do after university?
Yes, I'm hoping to become a tour guide because I love meeting people and sharing our history.
That sounds great! The tourism sector is really booming now. What skills would you need?
To succeed in tourism, you'd need to speak several languages and be really good at communicating.
Makes sense. I'm particularly interested in renewable energy, especially solar power projects.
Really? That's a smart choice. What's your plan?
By the time I'm 25, I'll have finished my engineering degree and gained some work experience at a solar company.
Wow, you've clearly thought it through! I'd better start making a plan too.

grammar.title: Future Perfect: By the time ..., I'll have ...
grammar.ar: نستخدم المستقبل التام (will have + التصريف الثالث للفعل) للتحدث عن شيء سيكون قد اكتمل قبل وقت معين في المستقبل. غالبًا ما نستخدم معه عبارات مثل by the time أو by 2030. لاحظ أن الفعل بعد by the time يكون في المضارع البسيط وليس المستقبل، فنقول: By the time I'm 25 وليس By the time I will be 25.
examples: By the time I'm 25, I'll have completed my master's degree.
By 2030, Saudi Arabia will have built many new tourist destinations.
By the time I finish school, I'll have learned how to code in three languages.

words.ex: She won a scholarship to study medicine in Canada.
One consequence of studying abroad is that you become much more independent.
A sustainable city uses clean energy and produces very little waste.
If I were in charge of the school, I'd make the breaks longer.
The new metro in Riyadh will make public transport much easier to use.
When the coach offered him a place on the team, he seized the opportunity.

dialogue.t: Suppose you could study anywhere in the world – where would you go?
Hmm, if I had the chance to study abroad, I would go to Japan to learn about robotics.
Japan? That would mean learning Japanese, though. Isn't that really difficult?
It is, but I'd seize the opportunity anyway. What about you?
Actually, I'd rather design a new city. If I were in charge of planning it, I'd make it completely sustainable.
Interesting! What would you do about cars?
I'd ban most cars and build excellent public transport instead. That would mean cleaner air for everyone.
I love that idea, but some people might complain at first!

grammar.title: Second Conditional for Imaginary Situations
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثانية للتحدث عن مواقف خيالية أو غير مرجحة في الحاضر أو المستقبل. تتكون من: If + الماضي البسيط، ثم would + الفعل المجرد. مع الفعل to be نستخدم were مع جميع الضمائر في الأسلوب الرسمي، مثل If I were. ويمكن استخدام Suppose أو Imagine بدلًا من If لطرح أسئلة افتراضية.
examples: If I won a scholarship abroad, I would study engineering in Germany.
If I were in charge of the city, I'd plant thousands of trees.
Suppose you could change one thing about your school – what would you change?

words.ex: I really regret not practising more before the competition.

words.ar: عند النظر إلى الماضي / بعد فوات الأوان
words.ex: In hindsight, I should have chosen the science club instead of the drama club.
Failing that test was a hard lesson learned about the importance of revision.
I used to take my grandparents' advice for granted, but now I value it.
I wish I had made the most of my summer holiday instead of staying indoors.
Joining the debate team was a turning point in my life.

dialogue.t: Is there anything you'd do differently if you could go back a few years?
Definitely. Looking back, I should have joined the coding club when I had the chance.
Why didn't you?
I was too shy. If I had joined, I would have made some great friends and learned so much.
I understand. I wish I had spent more time reading instead of playing video games every evening.
Do you think it affected you?
A little, but that experience taught me that small daily habits really matter in the long run.
That's a mature way to see it. Regrets are useful if we learn from them.

grammar.title: Third Conditional, I wish + Past Perfect, should have
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الثالثة (If + الماضي التام، ثم would have + التصريف الثالث) للتحدث عن موقف في الماضي لم يحدث ونتيجته الخيالية. ونستخدم I wish + الماضي التام للتعبير عن الندم على شيء حدث أو لم يحدث في الماضي. أما should have + التصريف الثالث فتعني أنه كان من الأفضل فعل شيء لكننا لم نفعله.
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
I wish I had listened to my teacher's advice.
Looking back, I should have asked for help much earlier.

words.ex: First, I'll briefly outline the main points of my talk.
Each main point should be supported by an example.
Good signposting helps the audience follow your presentation easily.
Try to keep your audience interested by asking them a question.
Making eye contact shows that you are confident and engaged.
To sum up, setting clear goals is the first step to success.

dialogue.t: Can you help me plan my two-minute talk? I don't know how to start.
Sure. Start with a clear opening, like: Today I'd like to talk about my goal of becoming a pilot.
Good. Then what?
Outline your structure. Say something like: I've divided my talk into three parts: why, how and when.
Okay. So, firstly, I'll explain why I love flying. Secondly, I'll describe the training I need. Finally, I'll share my timeline.
Perfect. And use linking phrases between parts, for example: This brings me to my next point: the training.
That sounds much more organised. Should I memorise everything?
No, just use short notes and remember to make eye contact with your audience.

grammar.title: Signposting and Sequencing Language
grammar.ar: عبارات الإرشاد هي كلمات وجمل تساعد الجمهور على متابعة تنظيم العرض، مثل Firstly وSecondly وFinally وThis brings me to my next point. نستخدمها في البداية لعرض خطة الحديث، وبين الأجزاء للانتقال بسلاسة، وفي النهاية للتلخيص. لاحظ أن عبارة I'd like to تعني أود أن، ويأتي بعدها الفعل المجرد.
examples: Today I'd like to talk about my dream of opening a café.
Firstly, I'll explain my goal; secondly, I'll describe my plan; finally, I'll discuss the challenges.
This brings me to my next point: how I'm going to save money.

words.ex: Our proposal is to create a youth club with a science lab and a gym.
She managed to convince the principal to start a robotics club.
The main benefit of the app is that it connects students with mentors.
Membership should be affordable so that every teenager can join.
We could get funding from local businesses and sponsors.
Let me address your concern about safety.

dialogue.t: Imagine how much more active teenagers would be if every neighbourhood had its own youth club.
Interesting. What exactly are you proposing?
A club with a sports hall, a gaming zone and a quiet study room. This would allow young people to develop new skills after school.
But how would you pay for it? Funding is always a problem.
That's a great question – the answer is partnerships with local companies, plus a small, affordable membership fee.
And what if teenagers just stay at home on their phones instead?
Let me address that concern. We'd organise competitions and events that they can't experience online.
Hmm, you've almost convinced me!
I'm convinced that this club will make our community healthier and more connected.

grammar.title: allow / enable / encourage + object + to-infinitive
grammar.ar: الأفعال allow (يسمح) وenable (يمكّن) وencourage (يشجع) تأتي بعدها مفعول به ثم to + الفعل المجرد. هذا التركيب مفيد جدًا في الإقناع لأنه يوضح فوائد المقترح. انتبه: لا نقول allow young people develop بل allow young people to develop. ونستخدم would قبلها للتحدث عن نتيجة متوقعة لمقترح لم يتحقق بعد.
examples: This app would allow students to find tutors quickly.
The club would enable young people to learn new skills for free.
Our events would encourage teenagers to spend less time on screens.

words.ex: My vision is a country where every young person can follow their passion.
I want to contribute to my country's development by becoming a doctor.
Vision 2030 aims to diversify the economy beyond oil.
Hard work and patience will help you achieve your goals.
After the presentation, we each completed a short self-evaluation.
He delivered his presentation clearly and confidently.

dialogue.t: In conclusion, I believe that young Saudis will help diversify the economy through technology and innovation.
The main message I want to leave you with is this: our future depends on the skills we build today.
Thank you for listening – are there any questions?
Yes, that was excellent. How exactly do you plan to contribute to your country's future?
I plan to study artificial intelligence and develop apps that improve healthcare in rural areas.
Impressive. How do you feel your presentation went?
Quite well, I think. But if I did this again, I would speak more slowly and make more eye contact.
That's a very honest self-evaluation. Well done!

grammar.title: Reflecting and Concluding: If I did this again, I would ...
